questions.question: Which law was developed in the 1600s to describe that any force applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions, regardless of the shape of the container?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pascal's Law**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pascal's Law** states that when an **external pressure is applied to an enclosed fluid**, the **pressure is transmitted equally throughout the fluid and to the walls of the container**, regardless of the shape of the container or the amount of fluid.
 
• **Blaise Pascal**, a **French **scientist and mathematician, **formulated the principle** around **1647**.
 
• Pascal's Law remains a fundamental principle in fluid mechanics and has countless applications in various fields, such as **hydraulics**, **engineering**, and even everyday tools like syringes and brakes.
 
 
• The **sphygmomanometer**, the device used to **measure your blood pressure**, relies on Pascal's Law to transmit the pressure fluctuations in your arteries to the mercury column or digital display.
 
• **Scuba diving gear**: The pressure experienced by divers increases with depth, and Pascal's Law ensures equal pressure distribution on all parts of the diver's body and equipment, maintaining comfort and safety.
 
• **Hydraulic lifts**: Cars are lifted at service stations, heavy machinery is raised in construction, and even dump trucks rely on Pascal's Law to transmit force through fluids, amplifying small forces into significant lifting power.
 
• **Hydraulic brakes**: The force you apply to your car's brake pedal is multiplied through a hydraulic system, transmitting pressure evenly to the brake pads on each wheel, creating powerful stopping force.
 
• **Hydraulic presses**: Compressing objects like bales of hay, forging metals, and shaping car parts utilizes hydraulic presses that harness the pressure multiplication principle.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Magnus's Law** deals with lift generation by a spinning object in a moving fluid.
 
• **Graham's Law** explains the diffusion of gases at different rates based on their molecular weight.
 
• **Torricelli's Law **relates the speed of an effluxing liquid to the square root of its height.

__
 
• **Bokajan** is a cement plant **located **in the **Karbi Anglong district of Assam**, situated approximately 21 kilometers from Dimapur Airport and 350 kilometers from Guwahati.

• **Cement**: 

 
 
• It is a **binding material** that hardens when mixed with water, sand, and gravel to form concrete.

questions.question: Which of the following aggregates best describes the National Income?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**NNP at FC**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **NNP at FC** (Net National Product at factor cost) **best describes **the **National Income**.
 
• It's calculated by deducting depreciation from GDP at MP, giving a more accurate picture of the net value of production.
 
• Net National Product at Factor Cost or** NNPFC** : It is the** net value of all the final goods and services that are produced by the residents of a nation within a period of one year**.
 
• It can be shown as
 
 
• 
 
**NNPFC** = **GNPMP - Net Indirect Taxes - Depreciation**.

 
 
 
 
• National income of a country means the sum total of incomes earned by the citizens of that country during a given period, over a year.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** at **Market Price** or **GDP****MP** :It is the gross market value of all final goods and services that is produced within the domestic territory of a nation within an accounting year.

 
 
• 
 
It is shown as: **GDPMP** = **Net domestic product at FC (NDPFC) + Depreciation + Net Indirect tax**.

 
 
 
 
• 
 
**Net Domestic Product (NDP)** at **Market Price** or **NDPMP** :It is the net market value of all the final goods and services produced within the domestic territory of the nation within a year excluding depreciation

 
 
• 
 
**​​Gross National Product (GNP)** at **Factor Cost** or **GNPFC** :It is referred to as the gross money value of all the final goods and services that are produced by the residents living within the boundaries of a nation during one accounting year excluding the net indirect taxes. 

 
 
• 
 
It is shown as: **GNPFC** = **GNPMP - Net Indirect Taxes**.

 
 
 
 
• National income is calculated using various methods, such as the output method, income method, and expenditure method.
 
 
• The output method measures national income by adding up the value of all goods and services produced in the country, while the income method measures it by adding up all the income earned by individuals and businesses in the country.
 
• The expenditure method measures national income by adding up all the spending on goods and services by households, businesses, and the government.
 
• The income method measures all the income earned by all the factors of production in an economy.

questions.question: In 1851, who discovered the phenomenon of Eddy currents which flow in closed loops within conductors in planes perpendicular to the magnetic field?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Leon Foucault**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **1851**, **Leon Foucault**, a **French** physicist, **discovered **the phenomenon of** Eddy currents**.
 
• He demonstrated that **when **a **conductor moves through a magnetic field or vice versa**, an **electric current is induced within the conductor**, forming closed loops perpendicular to the magnetic field.
 
• **These currents** are **known **as **Eddy currents** and can have various **effects**, including:
 
 
• **Generating heat**: The flow of Eddy currents within conductors results in energy loss as heat. This can be detrimental in some applications like transformers and motors.
 
• **Damping motion**: Eddy currents can induce a drag force on moving conductors in a magnetic field, slowing down their motion. This effect is used in magnetic brakes and damping mechanisms.
 
• **Creating repulsion forces**: Repulsive forces arise between a magnet and a conductor experiencing Eddy currents due to the interaction of their magnetic fields.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **British-American** inventor, practical experimenter, and music professor **David Edward Hughes** is well-known for his contributions to the **development **of the **printing telegraph **and the **microphone**.
 
• **American **physicist **Charles Hard Townes** worked on** quantum electronics **related to both **maser **and **laser devices**, as well as the theory and implementation of the maser, for which he was granted the foundational patent.
 
• **Nikola Tesla **was a **Serbian-American** inventor, futurist, and mechanical and electrical engineer.
 
 
• His contributions to the present **alternating current (AC) energy delivery system's design **are what made him most famous.

questions.question: What is the name of a type of waterfall with an enormous volume of water?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cataract**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cataract**:

 
 
• This term specifically refers to **a large, powerful waterfall with an enormous volume of water flowing over a steep drop**.
 
• Examples include **Niagara Falls**, **Victoria Falls**, and **Iguazu Falls**.
 
• The waterfall is **known for **having one of the **highest flow rates of any in the world**.
 
 
• In 2014, **Iguaçu Falls** recorded an all-time high in its flow rate, carrying 46,300 cubic meters per second - 33 times the usual water flow rate—after torrential rains.
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cascade**:

 
 
• ​While distinct from other types, cascade waterfalls are **similar to multi-step waterfalls**. This waterfall cascades over a set of rock stairs, but unlike multi-step waterfalls, it lacks plunge pools at each step.
 
• This type is one of the more **common **along** seasonal creeks in hilly or mountainous areas**.
 
• **Roaring Fork Falls** in the **Pisgah National Forest **of western **North Carolina** is a perfect **example **of a cascade waterfall.
 
 
 
• **Rapid**:
 
 
• ​This term typically** refers to fast-flowing sections of a river with turbulence** and whitewater, not necessarily large waterfalls.
 
 
 
• **Chute**:
 
 
• ​This refers to **a steep incline over which water flows quickly**, often associated with artificial structures like hydroelectric dams.
 
 

90:T

questions.question: Indian Councils Act of _______ also called Morley-Minto Reforms, series of reform measures enacted in the British Parliament
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1909**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Indian Councils Act of 1909** also called Morley-Minto Reforms.
 
• **Important** reform **measures **enacted under it are:
 
 
• The legislative councils at the Centre and the provinces increased in size.
 
• Central Legislative Council – from 16 to 60 members.
 
• Legislative Councils of Bengal, Madras, Bombay, and United Provinces – 50 members each.
 
• Legislative Councils of Punjab, Burma, and Assam – 30 members each.
 
• The legislative councils at the Centre and the provinces were to have four categories of members as follows:
 
 
• Ex officio members: Governor-General and members of the executive council.
 
• Nominated official members: Government officials who were nominated by the Governor-General.
 
• Nominated non-official members: nominated by the Governor-General but were not government officials.
 
• Elected members: elected by different categories of Indians.​ 
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Government of India Act 1935

 
 
• There was a growing demand for constitutional reforms in India by Indian leaders.
 
• India’s support to Britain in the First World War also aided in British acknowledgment of the need for the inclusion of more Indians in the administration of their own country.
 
• The Act was based on
 
 
• Simon Commission Report
 
• The recommendations of the Round Table Conferences
 
• The White Paper published by the British government in 1933 (based on the Third Round Table Conference)
 
• Report of the Joint Select Committees.
 
 
 
 
 
• Government of India Act, 1919
 
 
• The matters, which were of National importance or related to more than one province were governed at the central level, such as Foreign Affairs, Defence, Political Relations, Communication, Public Debt, Civil and Criminal Laws, Wire services, etc.
 
• The Central Legislature was made more powerful and more representative by this Act.
 
• The Act introduced a bicameral legislature; the Lower House or Central Legislative Assembly and the Upper House or Council of State.
 
• The legislators, under the new reforms, could now ask questions and supplementary, pass adjournment motions, and vote a part of the budget, but 75% of the budget was still not votable.
 
• The legislature had virtually no control over the Governor-General and his Executive Council.

questions.question: Which country came out with the first 'official' compilation of volleyball rules and was published by the YMCA?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The US**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The** first 'official' compilation of volleyball rules**, published **by **the **YMCA**, originated **in **the **United States**.
 
• **First Rules**:
 
 
• **Morgan **wrote down the original set of rules himself, containing basic **elements like a 6-foot 6-inch net**, the ability to use any number of players, and points scored from serving.
 
 
 
• **YMCA and Official Rules**:
 
 
• Recognizing the potential of the game, the **Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA)** formalized the rules and published them in the** "Handbook of the Athletic League of the Young Men's Christian Associations of North America"** in **1897**.
 
• This marked the first official compilation of volleyball rules.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **History of Volleyball**:

 
 
• In 1895, William G. Morgan, a physical education director at the YMCA in Holyoke, Massachusetts, invented volleyball as an indoor sport for businessmen seeking a less vigorous alternative to basketball.
 
• He initially called it "mintonette," but a professor later suggested the name "volleyball" due to the volleying nature of the game.
 
 
 
• Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA):
 
 
• ​The **YMCA**, **often known **as the **Y **in some regions, is a global youth organization with over 64 million members across 120 countries.
 
• Its **headquarters **are in **Geneva**, **Switzerland**.
 
• **George Williams** **established **the organization as the Young Men's Christian Association on **June 6, 1844**, in **London**.
 
• The group strives to develop a healthy body, mind, and spirit in order to live out Christian principles.

questions.question: Velocity of circulation of money is ______

options.text: k times the value of transactions
the number of times a unit of money changes hands during the unit period
the number of times the same transactions can be repeated by a given volume of money supply
the ratio of money balance to the value of transactions

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**the number of times a unit of money changes hands during the unit period**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Velocity of circulation of money** is defined as the **number of times a unit of money changes hands during the unit period**.
 
• It is the frequency with which the total money supply in the economy turns over in a given period of time.
 
• It is **measured **by **dividing GDP by the country's total money supply**. A high velocity of circulation in a country indicates a high degree of inflation.
 
• It helps in **determining how vigorous** a **country's economy** is.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The desire to hold financial assets in the form of money, such as cash or bank deposits rather than investments, is known as the **demand for money**.

 
 
• It refers to the **amount of money people want to hold at a given point**.
 
 
 
• **Hot money** signifies **currency that quickly and regularly moves between financial markets**, that ensures investors lock in the highest available short-term interest rates.
 
 
• It continuously shifts from countries with low-interest rates to those with higher rates.
 
• **FPI **(Foreign portfolio investment - investments made in securities and other financial assets issued in another country) is often referred to as** “hot money”** because of its **tendency to flee** **at the first signs of trouble in an economy**.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT true about green revolution?

options.text: It was funded by international agencies.
It was a private-sector programme for agricultural modernization.
It was targeted mainly in the wheat and rice-growing areas.
It was introduced only in areas that had assured irrigation.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It was a private-sector programme for agricultural modernization**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• 
 
The Green Revolution in India:

 
 
• The Green Revolution, which refers to the large-scale introduction of high-yielding varieties of seeds, fertilizers, and pesticides in agriculture, has been criticized for its negative impact on small farmers.
 
• The Government of India launched the Green Revolution in 1965 under the Third Five-Year Plan(1961-66).
 
• MS Swaminathan is considered the father of the Green Revolution in India.
 
• Norman Borlaug is known as the 'Father of Green Revolution' in the world.
 
• In India, the aim of this revolution was to increase the productivity of agricultural crops, particularly wheat and rice.
 
 
• The main focused crops were Wheat, Rice, Jowar, Bajra and Maize.
 
 
 
• In the first phase of the Green Revolution, the use of HYV seeds was limited to the more prosperous states of Haryana, Punjab, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Western Uttar Pradesh.
 
• HYV seeds refer to high-yielding varieties of seeds that were developed during the Green Revolution to increase crop yields.
 
 
• These are resistant to insects and diseases and have a high yield capacity.
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Green Revolution was a period of agricultural transformation that took place in the 1960s and 1970s in India.
 
• The goal of the Green Revolution was to increase agricultural productivity and food security by introducing high-yielding crop varieties (HYV seeds), modern irrigation systems, and chemical fertilizers and pesticides.
 
• It was a significant success in India, as it helped to increase agricultural output (especially wheat and rice) and reduce food shortages.
 
• However, it also had some negative impacts, such as environmental degradation, soil erosion, and the loss of traditional farming practices.

questions.question: Which of the following posts of Defence Research Development Organisation (DRDO) is in the Level I (top level) of its organisational chart?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Secretary DD and R & D**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Secretary DD and R & D:**

 
 
• This position, **also known** as the **Chairman of DRDO**, occupies the** highest level (Level I) **in the organizational chart.
 
• They are responsible for the overall leadership, direction, and control of DRDO's activities.
 
 
 
• **Director General Technical Cluster**:
 
 
• This position falls under** Level II **of the DRDO chart and reports to the Secretary DD and R & D.
 
 
 
• **Director General Corporate**:
 
 
• Similar to the DG Technical Cluster, this position is also in** Level II** and reports to the Secretary DD and R & D.
 
 
 
• **Director of Laboratory**:
 
 
• This position sits at **Level III **in the DRDO hierarchy and reports to the relevant Director General (Technical or Corporate) depending on the laboratory's area of expertise.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Defence Research and Development Organization (DRDO):

 
 
• It is the** R&D wing of the Ministry of Defence**, Govt of India, with a vision to **empower India with cutting-edge defence technologies** and a mission to achieve self-reliance in critical defence technologies and systems, while equipping our armed forces with state-of-the-art weapon systems and equipment by requirements laid down by the three Services.
 
• It was **formed **in 1958 from the amalgamation of the then already functioning Technical Development Establishment (TDEs) of the Indian Army and the Directorate of Technical Development & Production (DTDP) with the Defence Science Organisation (DSO).
 
• Its **headquarters **is DRDO Bhavan in **New Delhi**.
 
• Its Motto: "Balasya Mulam Vigyanam"(बलस्य मूलं विज्ञानम्) meaning the "source of strength is science" which will drive the nation in peace and war.
 
• The current (as on Jan 2024) **Chairman **of DRDO is Dr. Sameer V. Kamat.

questions.question: Bailadila range of hills are famous for which of the following minerals?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iron ore**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Bailadila Range** is a mountain range located in the **Dantewada district of Chhattisgarh**, India.
 
• It is known for its** rich deposits of iron ore**, which are among the highest grade in the world.
 
• The range is also home to a variety of plant and animal life, including tigers, elephants, and sal trees. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Iron ore**:

 
 
• The Ballary-Chitradurga-Chikmagalur-Tumkur belt located in Karnataka is renowned for its vast reserves of iron ore.
 
• It is considered one of the major iron ore belts in India, contributing significantly to the country's iron and steel industry.
 
• The Kudremukh mines, located in the Western Ghats of Karnataka, are entirely focused on exports.
 
• A pipeline carries the ore in a slurry form to a port close to Mangalore.
 
• One of the three main iron ore belts is the one that runs through Odisha and Jharkhand.
 
 
• The other two are the Bellary-Chitradurga-Chikmagalur-Tumkur belt and the Durg-Bastar Chandrapur belt.
 
 
 
• The Odisha-Jharkhand belt's Badampahar mines produce high-grade hematite ore.
 
 
 
• Manganese ore can be found in the districts of Balaghat, Chhindwara, and Jhabua in Madhya Pradesh, in Nagpur and Bhandara in Maharashtra and Sundargarh, Koraput, and Ganjam in Odisha.
 
• The five l**argest zinc mines in India** are **Rampura **Agucha Mine, **Sindesar **Khurd Mine, **Zawar **Mine, **Kayad **Mine, and **Rajpura Dariba** Mine.
 
• In terms of states, **Odisha **alone is **responsible for 51% of the nation's bauxite resources**, with **Andhra Pradesh (16%)**, **Gujarat (9%)**, **Jharkhand (6%**), **Maharashtra (5%)** and **Madhya Pradesh** & **Chhattisgarh** (4% each) following.
 
 
• The East Coast bauxite deposits in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh contain the majority of the world's bauxite resources.

questions.question: The Battle of Karnal is known for the invasion of which of the following aggressors against India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nadir Shah**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Battle of Karnal** occurred in **1739**, when **Nadir Shah**, the ruler of the Afsharid dynasty of Persia, invaded India.
 
• He** defeated the Mughal army** **led **by **Muhammad Shah** at Karnal and subsequently sacked Delhi, the Mughal capital.
 
• This decisive victory marked the beginning of the decline of the Mughal Empire.
 
• **Afsharid Dynasty**:
 
 
• The **Turkoman Afshar tribe** in **Iran's northeastern area of Khorasan** gave rise to the Afsharid dynasty, which **controlled Iran (Persia) in the middle of the eighteenth century**.
 
• **Nadir Shah (Nader Shah Afshar)**, a brilliant military tactician who deposed the final Safavid dynasty member and crowned himself Shah of Iran, **founded **the **dynasty **in **1736**.
 
• Under Nader's leadership, Iran reached its widest point since the Sasanian Empire.
 
• At its height, it **controlled **portions of **Iraq**, **Turkey**, the **United Arab Emirates**, and **Oman **in addition to modern-day **Iran**, **Armenia**, **Georgia**, the **Azerbaijan **Republic, **Afghanistan**, **Bahrain**, **Turkmenistan**, **Uzbekistan**, and **Pakistan**, as well as portions of the **North Caucasus (Dagestan)**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ahmed Shah Abdali**:

 
 
• The **founder of the Durrani Empire** and the modern state of Afghanistan was Ahmad Shah Abdali, sometimes referred to as Ahmad Khan Abdali or **Ahmad Shah Durrani**.
 
• **After Nadir Shah passed away in 1747**, **Abdali **was selected to** take over **and attacked India on several occasions between 1748 and 1767.
 
• During this period, he **launched eight invasions of India**, conquered Punjab, and **defeated the Marathas** in the **Third Battle of Panipat in 1761**.
 
 
 
• **Shah Shuja**:
 
 
• The **second child** of Mughal Emperor **Shah Jahan** and Empress **Mumtaz Mahal **was Mirza Shah Shuja.
 
• He served as **governor** of both **Bengal **and **Odisha**; his **capital **was **Dhaka**.
 
• Following Shah Jahan's sickness in September of 1657, the brothers had a power struggle.
 
• **Shah Shuja** declared himself to be the Emperor, but **Aurangzeb **took the Dehli throne and dispatched Mir Jumla to bring Shuja under control.
 
• On January 5, **1659**, **Shuja lost** the** Battle of Khajwa**.
 
 
 
• **Nasir Khan**:
 
 
• While Nasir Khan **participated in rebellions against the Mughal Empire**, he wasn't involved in the Battle of Karnal.
